synopsis: The braking system’s sensor set remains unconfirmed, so radar is one option requiring investigation rather than a settled design choice [f2035, f6625]. Radar simulation requires wavelength-specific material data, often measured at 77 GHz, and a modeled processing chain; physical correlation remains necessary for signatures, multipath, mounting, clutter and interference [f3715, f4420, f1739, f493]. Evidence shows substantial fidelity limitations: a 2025 wheel-loader simulation required manual material tuning yet missed double reflections, one 2026 ray-tracing study produced about 12% of real point density, and no validated radar or camera dust model with a reported error metric was found [f4421, f4422, f3716, f254]. Historical haul-truck testing in 2004 recorded alarms during 94% of 618 reversals over seven days; the study reported in 2006 classified 18% of 580 alarms as false, 42% as nuisance and 40% as warranting action, with nuisance alarms associated with ignoring or disabling behavior [f3010, f3011, f5174, f5175, f3480]. Detection evidence does not establish braking performance: the 2005 Griffith study detected light vehicles at 75 m but did not study brake thresholds, and a single rear radar missed people near haul-truck rear tyres [f6368, f6369, f7039]. Radar-equipped commercial systems do not independently prove adverse-environment validation is solved, while site interoperability and radar interference remain Medium to High risks for which interface and radio-frequency coexistence tests are recommended [f1749, f11076, f11078].
